utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is November 10th, 2009, and I greet everyone here in the courtroom, the accused, the Defence counsel, General Beneta, and the members of the OTP, as well as everyone helping us. Ms. Alaburic, let me remind you that you have 24 minutes left, and you have the floor. I apologise. Thirty-six minutes, not twenty-four. Thirty-six.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to you. Good morning to my colleagues from the OTP, to my colleagues from the Defence counsels.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General Beneta. Good morning to the accused and everybody who is with us. General, we broke off yesterday when you were describing the information that you received about sabotage activities on the eve of Operation South. I will ask you to repeat and comment whether with regard to the location and the description of the events, it corresponds to reality. The first document is P1045, P1045. I'll repeat, 10145. All right, now the number is correct. This is the statement of a Prosecution witness. I will read out a paragraph from page 6 of the Croatian version, and in the English version it starts with paragraph 38 on page 6. And I will say which paragraph I'm skipping. The witness in this statement says that he was an HVO soldier and that he was isolated in early July 1993, and that he escaped from Dretelj. And he says, I quote: "We were able to reach my village and find some of the inhabitants of the village who had fled from the attack. We lived in the forest, and our families were helping us by bringing us what we needed to survive. We monitored the movements of the Croats in that area." I'm skipping one paragraph. I continue quoting: "We established contact with members of the Army of BiH from Blagaj because in our group of 24 there was one man, an active soldier, professional soldier, who was able to procure a radio and establish contact with the Bosnian Army. We, 20 or so, had rifles, and we went on foot to Blagaj to fetch more rifles."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the English text please be displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Our group grew with the arrival of people from Blagaj and Gubavica ..." So it is not "Dubravica" as is stated in the transcript, but Gubavica: "... so that then we were 70. On the 12th of July, 1993, we received an order by radio from the command in Mostar to cut through the road from Mostar to Capljina -- between Stolac and Capljina," correction. So I correct the transcript. Between Stolac, rather than Mostar, Stolac and Capljina. "We decided to launch an action in the surroundings of Domanovici, not far from Potkos," so Domanovici, not far from Potkos, "together with the people from Prenja and Bregava." So from Prenja and Bregava. "We knew that a similar action was being taken nearby Buna, Gubavica, and at the check-point nearby Pijesci," the village of Pijesci. "We took our positions at dawn on the 13th of July, 1993. We arrested all members of the units from Bivolje Brdo, and in the course of that action we didn't fire a single shot, nor was anybody wounded. Three soldiers were locked in the garage of Mujo Sose at Kremenac, that is, the garage of Mujo Sose. They were guarded by Hasan Sose. "I personally was at the front-line near Strmac, in another village. We were waiting for reinforcement that was promised to us by the command from Mostar. At 1500 hours, we received the order to retreat toward Blagaj. Although our action was successful, that was not acknowledged and we received no support. We had to retreat and walk to Blagaj, and the civilian population we had to leave to their fate."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General Beneta, with regard to the description of the events, the time, and the locations mentioned, does this correspond to the knowledge you had then about the activities of the Army of BiH at the Dubravica Plateau?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at the next document, P9935, on page 4 of the Croatian text, and on the English text it's paragraph 26 on page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. I cannot help noticing that this was an extremely leading question. You have put the whole story to the applicant -- to the witness, I'm sorry, and asked him whether he could confirm this, whether it was according to his experience, and I'm not quite sure what this actually means. Mr. Beneta, do you know that three people were locked up in Sose's garage, for instance? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no knowledge of that. My affirmative answer was about the locations mentioned in this material and the course of the action, and what we subsequently found out, that they had crossed the line and made contact with Blagaj, which was held by the Army of BiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you know about the person who was a witness here, whose name I don't know whether you have mentioned it, Ms. Alaburic? I do not see anything that he is protected. It would be Vilogorac. Do you know one Mr. Vilogorac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So, in fact, your knowledge about this is very vague. You could not confirm what the witness has said here, could you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that what the witness said has a foundation in the overall situation which I knew, but I don't know the witness, nor the details he mentioned. But I know about that area and the time and the events that went on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you were not fully aware of this event. This was quite obvious. At least I found this obvious. However, militarily, what the witness is saying, the witness whose extract of the statement was read to you, seems interesting, but there are other passages that weren't read to you, and maybe you could give us your military point of view. We see that on July 13th, a military action is underway, executed by the BH Army soldiers who were ordered by Mostar to carry out this operation. This operation is successful, at least this is what the witness says, since they were able to capture HVO soldiers without shooting at any time. However, they say that at 3.00 p.m., they received an order to withdraw, so they leave the area. And then the rest seems quite interesting, and I'm sure that maybe you can help us. This is what he says: "After our action, the Croats launched an offensive, and those who suffered were the civilians." And then he describes the suffering in the next sentence: "All Muslim inhabitants in the region, whatever their age or condition, were arrested, detained, and expelled." And later on he says that about 800 to 900 people sought shelter in the woods, and part of the population was sent to the Capljina cookie factory and then -- and after that was expelled. What happened exactly? The BH Army attacked, then withdrew, and the HVO then launched its own action. And the HVO action is actually to expel civilians. Militarily, I would like to know whether this is a normal line of action. Does this happen? After an enemy action, is there a possibility to capture the civilians and expel them? Is this a traditional -- a classical military conduct? Is this normal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot testify to the details as an eye-witness, but according to what I learned at the command post of Operations Group 1, the situation in the area of the 1st HVO Brigade, from the military point of view, was very problematic. They, in the command of the brigade, received information from minute to minute that almost all elements of their combat layout in the entire depth were being attacked, which made the commander very nervous, and rightly so, and he was rather surprised. The actions that were executed to resolve the situation and prevent further negative consequences obviously were of such a nature that the commander, being unable to judge from whom he was being threatened, and the combat activity had spread from the front-line to the entire depth of the area, it was in such a situation that he evacuated all population from the area and put it under his control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I understand your answer well, and it is quite important and I don't want to make mistakes when I will have to assess what you say, you are saying that given the military situation, which was difficult, the HVO, militarily-wise, was only able to move the civilian population out of this area in order to protect it; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I'm saying. But to say the whole truth, he also protected his own men from possible subsequent such activity. It is obvious from the statement, and it also coincides with my recollection, that these people who were attacking the HVO forces in the depth of the area were not all soldiers, strictly speaking. Most of them were armed and in civilian clothes, and they had dangerous intentions. And with regard to all that, I justify the commander's actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, but then the witness in this statement adds something else, and Ms. Alaburic did not mention it, but I will. This is what he says: "The people were taken in trucks by HVO soldiers to Podpetak to be expelled." And just listen to rest, because I believe that what he says is quite important: "They were sent down the 300 metres from the front-line, and from the bunkers, where I was on duty, we could see about 50 metres. We heard the HVO soldiers firing towards the expelled people who were walking towards our lines. Along with my friends, we were responsible for helping the people who were arriving." This witness says that the HVO let the -- disembarked the expelled people 300 metres from the front-line and told them, Move forward towards the front-line. But it also seems that the HVO shot at these people at the same time. And he goes on to say that on July 15th, he received the body of his cousin, Remza, who was 75 to 80 years old. Now, militarily-wise, could you tell us whether this is a normal conduct, whether it's normal to shoot at people that you are -- that you've asked to move forward towards friendly lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If I were the commander in question, I would not approve such conduct unless that had been approved by telephone, called the hot-line between the warring parties, or if such a request had been made to send the people towards them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will finish, but -- because our witness -- this witness is saying, and of course this is what the witness says - you weren't there, and neither was I - but this is what the witness says: "At the beginning of the expulsion from Buna to Blagaj, there were casualties every day, but later on HVO soldiers stopped firing systematically on the exiled people. I think that between July 13th and 16th, 1993, at least 50 people were killed, trampled to death, or died through exhaustion, and many others disappeared." So according to him, there were about 50 people who were expelled under these conditions and who actually died. But militarily-wise, in such an operation where the civilian population are to be protected, how can you explain this? How can you explain that some of the civilians were shot at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the military point of view, the only thing I can say, with knowledge of the situation down there from the reports, that I am not aware that so many people of Muslim ethnicity - that's probably who the witness means - had been killed. I know that over 20 members of that brigade had been killed, along with the civilians who happened to be in that area in this attack by Muslim forces. And I want to stress here, without going into the veracity of the witness's evidence, that it is very questionable whom we can consider as a civilian, if it concerns a person between the age of 18 and 60, of male gender, who could have been in possession of a weapon and would have been a military conscript, so it's quite possible that people from that brigade were over-sensitive to the possibility of a threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like first to correct the record. On line 12 of page 7, when the witness mentioned civilians, he said there were not civilians, strictly speaking, there were armed civilians. The witness actually said that these were armed people in civilian clothing, and that is an important distinction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm, General, that this is accurate?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just explain to Judge Trechsel that my question on lines 1 to 4, page 4, was very precise, because I know that the witness cannot know details such as the garage and similar, and my question was not leading, and I'll explain why. I asked him, in general terms, about the events, about the time mentioned in the statement, 12th and 13th July, and the locations mentioned in the statement. The witness told us yesterday that sabotage actions had taken place on the 12th and 13th July, which coincides with the timing in this statement, and there is also reference to place names, such as Domanovici, Gubavica, Bivolje Brdo, and other locations which are on the Dubrava Plateau, and the witness can confirm that, and that indeed there had been sabotage actions there. And in view of all the witness's evidence from yesterday, I thought that I could put such a question summarising the evidence from this statement. I think it would be now fair for me to explain why I had not read the entire statement, because this could be interpreted as an attempt to conceal a part of the statement. That's why I said to everyone in the courtroom that I would be using the statement so that the Judges and everyone else could look at it in its entirety. The subject of this evidence are the sabotage actions of the Bosnian Army. I did not want to go into what the HVO had or had not done. We did not have a witness in the courtroom to question about that. So I suppose that the Judges' questions referred to whatever can be assumed from the statement, assuming that it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I want that my question, whether the correction I made was accurate, that those were armed people in civilian clothing. Can you answer that again?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I emphasised in my answer that those were mainly people in civilian clothing who were armed and who constituted a danger to the members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Considering that there is this disagreement between the Prosecution and the Defence about those sabotage actions, their causes and consequences, I will continue the line of questioning to confirm that these sabotage actions had taken place. May I now move on to statement 9935, a witness statement, paragraph 26 in both Croatian and English. I quote: "According to my brother Mirsad, on the evening of 13 July 1993, young people from the village prepared an operation to liberate the region and to put a stop to the crimes committed against us by the Croats. I don't know whether this operation was coordinated with a wider-scale one conducted by the Bosnian Army. I think that the young villagers who had been hiding in the surrounding area were liaising with the Bosnian Army, but I don't know whether this planned operation was taken on their own initiative or it was directed from the outside by the army. I am aware that the objective of the operation was to attack the Croats, but it failed. And later on, my brothers no longer mentioned it." Let me just tell you, General, in the other passages, Domanovici and some other places on the Dubrava Plateau are mentioned. Now, concerning the location and the time referred to in this statement, are they consistent with your evidence given here about the sabotage actions by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is consistent with the picture I was getting from the reports I received at my command post during those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look now at some more documents. 4D1101. These will be HVO documents. 1101. This is a record of questioning drawn up based on an interview with Mr. Becir Suta. I'll summarise the whole statement quickly. It's short. It says that on the Dubrava Plateau, they had established a unit, and he says: "My group had the task to emerge at Masline to set up a line ..." And then he enumerates the members of the group, including Salko Alihodzic, and finally he says they had refused to shoot, and eventually they were found in that location by the HVO and they were brought in to the barracks. Now, this location, Masline, is it on the Dubrava Plateau, from what you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, 4D1096. It's an Official Note drawn up after interviewing a gentleman called Admir Cevra, and in the second paragraph it says: "In the course of an operation started by the BH Army, I was also in that hamlet, and people from that village, who were actively engaged in combat against the HVO, were Ahmet and Mithad Cevra ..." He also lists other people as having taken part in the clash with the HVO. And concerning Mithad, he said he had been a member of the HVO, Mostar. He did not get involved in the action. Instead, he helped the HVO detect the members of the army who were hiding in the vicinity of the village. Now, General, is this consistent with your knowledge about the members of the BH Army who were active in villages and other places around the Dubrava Plateau?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this also is consistent with what I know on a general level.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document, 4D1042. This is a report, a summary, made evidently on the basis of interviews with various participants in the action. I'll highlight certain parts. A group of 70 is mentioned, then a group of 50, and then there is reference to a meeting at Gubavica, where they had received a specific mission to take the barracks at Gubavica. Tell me, who had barracks at Gubavica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks at Gubavica is, in fact, a smaller installation that the former Yugoslav Army had used for some communications equipment. At that time, we had reports that it had been attacked. The attackers surrounded it quietly and then launched a sudden attack, and the people inside were captured due to a coincidence, because the surprise attack was made with anti-armour assets that would have normally destroyed the whole place. However, all these anti-armour vehicles got stuck in the wire fencing around the installation, so the people inside managed to repel the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which army was stationed inside this installation? Who was attacked?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a unit of the 1st Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Localities Dubrava is then mentioned, and a group of 15 soldiers; at Oplicici, a group of 50 soldiers was formed and given the task to neutralise HVO soldiers stationed in Satorova Gomila. Then it says an operations group of 25 to 30 people was established at Lokve village, with a task of cutting the road from Domanovici from Stolac. And then another group of 15 people is mentioned who had the task to cut off the road Domanovici-Bivolje Hill. Tell me, General, in view of the size of these groups and the localities where they were active, is that consistent with what you knew about the situation on the ground then?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is consistent with the reports that were coming in at the time. I know that fierce and long fighting took place at Satorova Gomila.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Further below in the text, it says that according to the statements of prisoners, the task was broadened and they were supposed to get reinforcement from Mostar, approximately 700 soldiers, with the objective of holding on to the territory they had taken control of and move on to Stolac and Capljina, taking complete control of the Dubrava Plateau. Does this surprise you or is it consistent with what you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was also our estimate of their intentions after we received the first reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll skip the next two documents, because I don't think it's important to see all five of them at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, 4D1042 is a document I would like to talk about still. This document stems from the Military Information Service, and out of interest I looked at the addressees of this document. There are three of them: The Defence Department of Mr. Stojic; the commander of the Operational Group 2, Matic; and the head of the department, Zarko Keza. This department receives information, first-hand information, from soldiers who have been captured and who describe what has happened. So an order by Arif Pasalic seems to have been given, and this plan will continue. He says, by way of a conclusion, that this will continue during the night and over the next few days. A military piece of information of this kind, according to you -- maybe you can't answer the question. I don't know. If you can't, let me know. How is it that this is not sent to the commander of the HVO in person, perhaps even to the Supreme Commander, the commander of the armed forces, Mate Boban, when this is being sent to the Defence Department and to the commander of Operation Group 2? Does this seem logical, in military terms? In a situation like this, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must admit that I don't know the exact structure and organisation of the HVO, and I didn't know it even then, so I cannot give -- really give you an informed answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's imagine - this is a textbook example - that your unit captures enemy soldiers who disclose the existence of a plan. Who would you have informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I put myself in the shoes of the person who signed the document, then I would have informed my superior officer. Who of these people mentioned is the superior officer, I don't know. We would have to look at the organisational structure. Perhaps somebody was in the field and another person in the staff, so he decided to inform whoever needed to know the information. But, again, I repeat, I cannot give you accurate information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let us return to Operation South. Tell us, what was the position of the commanders of the 1st and 3rd Brigades about the readiness and capability of the HVO for larger-scale military operations even before these sabotage actions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- the first knowledge I received about their capabilities and their readiness to engage in attack activities was when I was on command reconnaissance with Mr. Dzanko, and on that occasion we spoke to the commander of the 3rd HVO Brigade, Mr. Primorac, and it was his firm assertion that his unit does not have forces to keep such a long stretch of the confrontation line and, in addition, engage in attack activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, to your knowledge, who was it that, in spite of these views of military operations, approved the execution of Operation South?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in such talks. I was tasked with staff work in Operations Group 1. I cannot be certain who it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge about Luka Dzanko going somewhere to have meetings and take decisions with someone?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the operations group, Mr. Dzanko, went to Grude several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know, General, who had his office at Grude?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that, at that time, Mr. Boban had his office at Grude.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, General Petkovic, did he participate in the planning of this operation in any way; do you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have seen no document showing that, nor did I meet him in those days in the area in which I moved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that the operation was delayed to the 15th of July in 1993. Tell us, was it really executed on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the action began on the 15th, and it ended very soon and unsuccessfully.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Before the beginning of the operation, did a high-ranking officer or official of the HVO Army come anywhere close to the command post?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At dawn of the day of the launch of the operation, Mr. Boban came to the artillery positions not far from the Command of Operations Group 1. There were also some other people from the HVO whom I don't remember. They were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was it at that place or anywhere near that the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, General Milivoj Petkovic, was to be found?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To end with, General, let us look at two documents. 4D1695, 1695, that's a list of the members of the Command of Operations Group 1. Tell us, General, what kind of command was that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list of people from the command and others who were likely to come to the building of the command of the group of operations -- operations group. The list was given to the security services for them to know whom they were allowed to let into the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was this the Command of Operation South?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a list of the command of the operation and of persons who went to see the command frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And let us now look at the last document, P3048.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Beneta, have you seen this list before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this list during the proofing. These days, it was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you have an idea what date it was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This letter, judging by the persons mentioned, was made at the planning stage of the operation; that is, 'round about the 8th or 9th, possibly the 10th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Trechsel. This was really missing to make this document complete information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document. It doesn't have a date, so maybe you can tell us when it was drafted. So it's document P3048. It's an attack order. In the upper right-hand corner, it says "South," in inverted commas. Tell us, General Beneta, did you know this document before?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know this document. This is an order which was written once the decision had been taken, and it was drafted by the operations officers of the staff which I headed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, can you give us accurate information about the date when this document was produced?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 10th or the 11th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General Beneta.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a follow-up question of a technical nature, based on the last document. Operational Group 1 is going to be reinforced by HVO units or assisted by the HVO units which are mentioned. In this context, the command is exercised by the commander of the Croatian Army, and in that case, are the HVO units re-subordinated to the command of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Dzanko commanded this battle. Technically, he was an HV officer, but I believe that he was assigned to this task the same way I was; namely, that somebody had asked him to come and help out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take another textbook example. Let's assume that the HVO in a particular area needs the support of the Croatian Army. The HVO commander then asks the Croatian Army to be provided with some men, perhaps even an entire unit. In that particular case, who in the field will exercise operational command over the unit of the Croatian Army that would have been made available, seconded? Who in the field has authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if HV members came to help out, that means that somebody from the HVO was in command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that it is someone from the HVO who would be in command. This is what you're saying between the lines, if we take this textbook example. We shall now have a break and resume after the break with other Defence counsel. I have further questions. Perhaps other Defence teams would like to get ready. Normally speaking, we have a break at 10.30, but there's no set rule. The Bench decides it's in the interests of justice and for the proceedings. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you, Judge Antonetti, for these questions. And if you allow, I'll just ask one question, a follow-up question. Perhaps I should have put it, myself, earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Assuming, General Beneta, that Mate Boban, as the Supreme Commander of the HVO, decided whether or not the operation would be launched, what does that mean with regard to who the superior officer of Luka Dzanko, the commander of the operation, was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, he would be subordinate to Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer is interesting. But to illustrate what you've just said, I would like to state another case. You remember what happened in Kuwait when Iraq invaded Kuwait, and I'm sure you remember that the US Army had come to support Kuwait in that particular instance. Let's imagine, as a follow-up to Ms. Alaburic's question, that the commander of the US Army is there in Kuwait City. The commander of the Kuwaiti Army is also there. According to this situation, who would be in command of the military operations? Would it be the Kuwaiti commander or would it be the US commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the American Army came to help out, then the Kuwaiti commander is in charge. I don't want to go into what really happened, but the Kuwaiti commander should have commanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why you said that, normally speaking, it was Mate Boban who was in command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said as much also because I knew the situation as it was down there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question of a technical nature. When you were in the field, yesterday we saw a map, we saw where you were positioned, beyond Dubrovnik. What I would like to know is this: When you find yourself in such a situation, with your command in Zagreb, were you in permanent contact through radio communication, telex, faxes, with them or were there problems with the line of communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as a brigade commander at the time, I was subordinate to the commander of the south theatre of operations, and I had communication with them, with occasional breakdowns that occurred after moving, especially moving the command post, because the infrastructure was very bad and we had not enough radios, and part of the radios could not operate because of the hilly and mountainous terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are telling us that you were in communication with the command of the southern front, but you were not in direct communication with Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. In such situations that are very complex, militarily-wise, notably when an Army X is going to support Army Y, in order to avoid problem of collateral damage between Army X and Army Y, who by definition are friendly armies, should there be joint commands set up, or at least very sophisticated and high-performance communication system, to make sure that there is no friendly-fire problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That problem occurs more on the ground than on command level, and it's resolved by issuing specific tasks to the troops on the left and right flanks and points of coordination in terms of task, time, and space. The commands may be in various modes of cooperation, but it is much more important to ensure proper cooperation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question. You had command of a brigade, so between you and a unit on the ground, a small unit on the ground which is carrying out a pre-planned operation, could you tell us whether you were supposed to be in permanent contact with this unit so that you get feedback -- immediate feedback on successes that it has on the ground, that -- problems that it encounters on the ground, and so on? There's supposed to be permanent contact with the unit, this unit deployed on the ground, and yourself, as brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you probably mean a unit that is not an organic part of my brigade. In that case, it is highly desirable to answer, yes, that spares a lot of problems to the commander in charge of the operation. Life in war is much more complex than that. Sometimes you don't have enough devices, especially at that stage of the war. Sometimes you lose communication. Sometimes the devices that you have are not compatible with those that they have, and that created huge problems for liaison between units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for your answer, and I have one last question. You told us earlier that at one point in time, you had some casualties in one of your operations, killed and wounded troops. So when a brigade commander has casualties, is this commander supposed to ask his subordinate officers for a report on the circumstances that led to these troops being killed or wounded? Is this normal military conduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This should be an integral part of the report, how losses occurred. I must confess that those reports did not give much detail on whether a soldier died from a bullet, or from a shell or shrapnel, or in a car accident because a shell exploded close to the car, but the reports described the general military situation in which losses occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the enemy has casualties, do you also ask your own troops for a report to know how these enemy troops were killed? Is that done or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the same as with own losses. A description of the situation is given and the number of dead, without detailed explanation of how, except if the commander in charge of the unit has noticed something that one of his men had done something that runs counter to regulation or to international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me ask my fellow Judges whether they want to continue for 20 minutes or whether we should have the break right now. No, obviously we're going to continue until 10.30. I will now ask the other Defence teams to see what they want to do with the hour and 30 minutes that they have. D1.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and around. The Prlic Defence has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D2, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone. For the sake of our internal agreement, I must say that D2 team is the first in order to examine this witness. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What about 3D?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good, Your Honour. The 3D team does have questions. Specifically, General Praljak has military questions for the witness. He has prepared a large map that will be posted on the big board. Unfortunately, we did not have time overnight to photocopy it, so we would kindly ask your approval to prepare it for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, how long does General Praljak need, how many minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our schedule, each Defence team -- sorry, the Defence teams have an hour and a half, thus each Defence has 17 minutes. But since our colleague Suzana has no questions, we reckon that we would finish within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirty minutes. Very well. General Praljak, your counsel said you had 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours. May I ask the usher to distribute this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, to make sure we don't run into the same problems as last week, please keep an eye on the clock. You have been given 30 minutes. You shouldn't run over, because when you exceed the time allotted, we have problems. The second piece of advice. Please go to the crux of the matter, and if you have any time left, go to marginal issues. Don't do it the other way around. If you first deal with the marginal issues, you have no time left for the core issues. So please focus. And if you have any time left, then you can also deal with ancillary issues. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, General. Your Honours, since we did not have time to see each other in the break, I would like to inform that part of the questions from General Praljak refer to yesterday's record, pages 13 and 14 through 16. Those are the topics General Praljak wants to cover. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. There seems to be very little generosity towards me, a minute here or a minute there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't let you say this. Sometimes, you see, in just 15 seconds you can ask a question that sums everything up. You don't always need to spend a whole hour on issues. So don't say that you're not given enough time. You have been allotted 30 minutes, and focus on your -- on the right questions and everybody will be happy; you also. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Beneta -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] While I'm putting my questions, may I just ask this map to be hung?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Beneta, the Judge asked you about the cooperation between the Croatian Army and the HVO. In your first stint in the liberation of Stolac, did you go there as the Croatian Army, a Croatian officer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In that second operation, Operation South, did you ask, be it your zone commander or the commander of the south theatre of operations or someone in Zagreb, whether you could go? Did you go there privately, in other terms, or as a Croatian officer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there as an officer of the Croatian Army who agreed, of his own free will, to help out in the operation by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you ask Zagreb for permission to leave?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from that link you spoke about yesterday, using the map, between the HV and the HVO, do you know of any other case where a unit of the Croatian Army was re-subordinated to the HVO for a particular operation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. We have a problem, a common theatre of operations. Was the Yugoslav Army attacking Croatia separately and Bosnia-Herzegovina separately, or was it just invading whatever territory it wanted?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was working according to a central plan, regardless of the identity of the former Yugoslav Republic the operation was targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. From where was Vukovar attacked?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovar was attacked by the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army from areas which are now the Republic of Serbia and from the then occupied territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: From where was Okucani and Pakrac areas in Western Slavonia attacked, the occupied part of the territory we call Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces that attacked there had come from areas in what is now Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: To cut a long story short, does it apply also to attacks in Knin, Zadar, Sibenik, Dubrovnik? Look at the map.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in all these areas the army came and also received support, once it had come in, from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm interrupting because General Praljak is going into details and I'd like to keep a higher view of things. One thing is important, and he put a question to you on this but he didn't go into details. Could you tell us, according to you, whether Serbia had a general plan of attack encompassing Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and so on, or whether Serbia had a specific plan of attack to first attack Croatia, then move on to Bosnia-Herzegovina, or maybe first attack Bosnia-Herzegovina and then Croatia? According to you, what kind of plan of attack did the Serbians have -- the Serbs have? Was it a general plan of attack or was it specific, according to different republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the strategic level, the Serbs, in conjunction with the leadership of the Yugoslav People's Army, had as their ultimate goal reaching the line that, to their mind, would serve the interest of creating a Greater Serbia. The operational significance of the operations that were meant to implement the strategic idea were executed based on judgements of the situation on the ground. And they are subject to changes, but they are always done with a view -- or, rather, with the ultimate goal in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not directly answering my question, but it was a simple question, according to me. Either they have a general plan of attack or they have a plan which is broken down according to specific republics. This is what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I stand by my position that the general plan was in accordance with the ultimate goal, and the individual plans are an outcome of considerations how the ultimate goal can be achieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What you said is very important. I believe everyone understands. So if there is a general plan of attack which, according to you, corresponds to the final goal of the Serbs, which is to achieve a Greater Serbia, then, as far as the theatre of operations is concerned, it's a single theatre of operations, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the strategic level, it's a single theatre of operations or front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me repeat what you've said, because I believe it's quite important, and this has to be well recorded on the transcript. You said that according to you, there is a single theatre of operations; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the force that wanted to occupy -- I can't give an exact percentage, but let's say 70 per cent of former Yugoslavia, there was a single plan in place and a single theatre of war. For Croatia, and Slovenia, too, and somewhat later Bosnia-Herzegovina that tried to pull out of it, everybody had their own worries and went about them the way they could. They tried to oppose the idea which had come from one place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, you have the floor, but I believe it was important to highlight this issue. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Beneta, which borders in Croatia should the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army or the Serbian forces have reached? We don't have the map here, but --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, General, I can't show you that, but it's the well-known line that they mention in their memoirs and books, I mean texts authored by Serbian authors, and that's the line from Virovitica to Karlobag.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Virovitica-Karlovac-Karlobag.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: A follow-up question. In accordance with your overall military doctrine, did the attacked party, under the doctrine of the JNA, or NATO, whatever, have the right to oppose the attacking party anywhere and with whatever means, if they are able to do so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in the process it looks for allies to establish a balance at the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at the map of the south. You can see the date up there. Please read it out.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Disposition of forces on the 1st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know whether this was really the disposition of forces of the Yugoslav Army, as shown here?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This attack almost brought about the fall of Dubrovnik - it was only a matter of time - and it was cut off from the remainder of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that in the blocking defence of Dubrovnik, volunteers from Herzegovina also took part?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that applies also to other units. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, should we have a break now, and then I can use the remaining 15 or 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's almost 10.30, so let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Beneta, you had a look at the map. We can't give it to you now, but would you sign this map as something that reflects the facts at the time, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By the way, it was signed by a man whom I trust as much as I trust myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who signed it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Milan Perkovic, who analysed these activities when we were analysing what was happening in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you a volunteer in the Croatian Army or were you drafted in accordance with the mobilisation plans?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a volunteer in the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was General Petkovic drafted or was he a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In 1991, almost up until the recognition, what percentage of the Croatian Army was the share of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A huge percentage, almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Almost all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So until the recognition of Croatia, that is, January 1992. Mr. Prlic is pointing something out to me. So when was Croatia recognised by the European Union? Some countries recognised it earlier.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the recognition was on the 15th of January, 1992, and everybody who had joined the units earlier, even now, has -- enjoy the status of volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to hear the following now. After the end of the war, you worked in the Croatian Army, and you still work there. Among other things, you worked on the adjustment or the adaptation of the Croatian Army to NATO standards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: When I say "adaptation," I mean procedures, and the process of commanding, control, communication, joint activities, and, in a word, hundreds of algorithms that clearly outline what must be done in which situations, who is accountable to who, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Beneta, although the Croatian Army was already a full-fledged army then, how much time and effort was required for the system of the Croatian Army to be adapted to NATO standards?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have worked on that since the end of the war intensively -- correction. We started to work on that intensively in 1999, and the work still is not completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, what kind of procedures were in place, generally speaking, in the Croatian Army in 1991 which consisted mostly of volunteers? Could they be considered satisfactory, as compared to JNA standards or any other standards, or could we boil them down to the phrase "adapt and defend yourself"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to speak about accepted procedures in the armed forces. The question was not whether the procedures as known from the JNA at the time would be implemented, or NATO procedures, for that matter. The issue was how many men you have in your unit, men who you can entrust with commanding others, bearing in mind the fact that they had no command experience whatsoever. The first unit at battalion level that I established, established with two officers who had command experience, and that was myself and my deputy, Milan Perkovic, who signed this map. Nobody else had military experience, apart from doing their military service and knew how to fire a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, was the situation possibly even worse at other places, say in Vukovar, Mitnica, Borovo Naselje, Trpinjska road, et cetera? The people there, were they just guys who gathered and defended themselves?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I can remember four or five men who had a previous military career and command experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: While fighting is ongoing and when there is no time, is a verbal order as good as a written order?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: We are coming close to the end. Let's look at document, in this file, P03983. Were you aware, General Beneta, that at a certain period I was commander of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were you aware that my deputy was General Petkovic and the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO was General Tole?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About Mr. Tole, I cannot confirm, but about Mr. Petkovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you aware of the order in the Main Staff prevailing concerning who has the right to command?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look at this document, item 2. You see this specifies who would actually, in the circumstances prevailing on the 29th September 1993, and you can see my signature -- no, no, sorry, this is the wrong document. I asked for P05468. That's the next document. I misspoke. A leading group on duty has been determined to deal with all the issues of combat readiness, all urgent issues, commands and directs the immediately subordinate commands, et cetera. Mr. Beneta, you were not really aware of this, but if the situation so requires and you are unable to change the situation, would you adapt the command, rather than stick to your fixed system that would entail losses of men and territory?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commander is expected to adjust to the situation, because within the framework of general criteria of command, it is more important to achieve the task, fulfill the mission, rather than stick blindly to one mode or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel asked you yesterday what exactly is Herzegovina here. Therefore, I'd ask you, on this map of Bosnia and Herzegovina that you will receive now --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher to take this map and put it on the ELMO. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: On this map, General, you will outline roughly Herzegovina, and you will write "Eastern Herzegovina" "Western Herzegovina." And then you will also write "Central Bosnia," and then "Western Bosnia" or "Bosnian Krajina," "Western Bosnia," and "Eastern Bosnia." Let us have the outlines of various regions for the benefit of the Judges. Take this pen, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Place this part, Herzegovina, on the ELMO so we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What is to the right of Mostar -- to the east or to the right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eastern Herzegovina [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Put "1."

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What is to the west of Neretva River?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the west of the Neretva River [marks] is Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you include Tomislavgrad and Livno?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll draw the line there, because they had not agreed whether they are or not a part [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Put "2" there, and mark Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Shall I put "3"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Now mark Bosnian Posavina. You don't need to be so precise.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now mark Western Bosnia or Bosnia Krajina.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And the central part can be called, altogether, Central Bosnia; is that it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now please sign this map and put the date.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have an IC number for the map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document just marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC1100. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not signed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please sign it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Judge Antonetti, may I ask you that tomorrow, when we get a photocopy of this map, enable the witness, please, because I couldn't do it this morning, to get an IC number for this map, for the photocopied map. I think I finished in less than 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Beneta, thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm puzzled again. The map previously that the witness referred to and signed - do you remember, he said it had been signed by somebody that he trusted as much as himself - according to what I understood from Judge Trechsel the other day, because he didn't put any marking on it, it doesn't get an IC number. But I'm still extremely puzzled, Your Honour, because if it doesn't, then what happens to it? Because he's referred to it in evidence, it is in some sense incorporated in evidence, but it's sort of lost in space, and I just remain absolutely puzzled as to how the system, as described to me from the Bench the other day, with respect, makes any sense at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, the map, would you be asking for an IC number for this map or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the beginning of the cross-examination by General Praljak, we explained that it had been made in haste overnight and we had no time to photocopy. Now, if we get an IC number now, we would lose the map. We asked for time to photocopy it and give an IC number to the photocopy, because the witness spoke about it in his evidence, he knows the author very well, as he said, and we have all the elements needed for the identification, and the reliability of data indicated on the map has been established. However, since it's the only map the general has, we cannot let go of it, but we could tomorrow. We are sending it to be photocopied today. While I'm on my feet, Your Honours, the numbers 4 has not been -- have not been recorded. When General Praljak examined about the positions, that is, locations of various regions such as Western and Eastern Herzegovina, the witness answered these questions, but the record does not show the numbers given by the witness to denote the various parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could we just add this to the record? Number 3 was placed. Bosnian Posavina should have been marked. The witness marked it. Bosnia -- in fact, Bosnian Krajina was marked, as well as Central Bosnia, but these numbers are not on the record. And now, for the record, I just want to confirm that these were regions referred to by the witness, which means number 4 should be Bosnian Posavina. Am I right? You can no longer remember. The evidence follows the numbers. 4 was Bosnian Posavina, 5 was Western Bosnia, and then Central Bosnia was number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make it clear, Your Honour? I completely agree with what Ms. Pinter says. As far as the timing of the marking of IC numbers is concerned, clearly that's a sensible, practical solution. My concern had been that the rigorous application of the system, as described to me the other day, would have meant that this document got no IC number ever. As long as it's going to get one, the problem is solved. And clearly, because I'm quite sure that the document wouldn't be disgorged once it had disappeared into the moor of the Court with an IC number, it's sensible that it should be retained for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, according to what I've understood, the map we have, well, is a map that General Praljak only obtained during the night, so your colleague was unable to photocopy this map for all and every one. If we are able to give an IC number to this map already, then the Registrar can take the map, because he's custodian of this document. So to avoid that happening, your colleague suggests that tomorrow -- because in the afternoon she will make the photocopies, and then officially she will ask for the map to be given an IC number tomorrow. This is what I have understood, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm happy to say, as a matter of fact, that is, with respect, exactly what I had understood, Your Honour, when I was on my feet a few minutes ago. That was my understanding, and I'm most grateful to Your Honour for confirming that the understanding I had had was, in fact, correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Beneta, a moment ago -- well, I have a follow-up question for you, because General Praljak put a question to you, and you said that the Croatian Army, the HV, was made up of volunteers, and at the time there were no conscripts. This is what I have understood, that the Croatian Army at the time, in the years 1992, 1993, and following years, was made up solely of volunteers. Is that how we should understand what you have told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, up to the international recognition of the Republic of Croatia, anyone who had spent 100 days in the battle-field up to the 15th of January, 1992, is still considered today as having the status of volunteer, which means that to qualify for that status, a person had to join the armed forces up to the end of September, thus earning 100 days before the recognition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, the Croatian Army, unless I am mistaken, is made up of 17.000 troops, 50.000 reservists, and 1 million able-bodied men, 850.000 of which would be fit to be combatants. I believe that your budget amounts to in excess of 2 million -- 2 per cent of the GDP, given that your budget decreases over the years. I don't know why that is the case, but your defence budget decreases over the years. On the 15th of January, 1992, you say that there was a change then, and the Croatian Army, if I understand correctly, was also made up of conscripts. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you say that at the time, those people that had spent 100 days on the front-line retained their status as volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Men who had spent 100 days in the battle-field up to the 15th of January have the status of volunteer, in terms of certain benefits they now enjoy from Croatia. With the establishment of units, they became part of these units, and their status has no relation to their service in units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have told us that you were in charge of streamlining the Croatian Army with NATO standards. You, better than anyone else, you are aware of the fact that this status as a volunteer is not something which exists in Western armies in the 1990s because conscription was the rule, that drafting was the rule, so which is -- we find it difficult to understand what a volunteer actually means. Over the last four years, we've been discussing this term, and we're beginning to put our finger on what it actually means to have the status of a volunteer. If I understand correctly, a volunteer was someone who decided, of his own free will, to join the army, without anyone ordering him to do so, and that is how you became a volunteer to go to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Am I mistaken when I say this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time we are discussing is a time when a state was being established, an army too, and a war is starting. Things that are normal in countries with a well-established political system are in good order. We were in the situation to simultaneously establish an army starting to fight in a war and establishing a state. If you want me to draw a parallel, I must say that that's extremely difficult to do. I believe that General Praljak is closest to the truth when he says that those of us who were in commanding positions, and I believe the same applies to high-ranking political officials, were endeavouring to do our very best, but the likelihood of making mistakes in such circumstances is much greater. Mistakes couldn't always be avoided, but we always tried to do the best that circumstances would allow us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask another question of you, Mr. Beneta. Before the break this morning, in answering a question of Mr. Praljak, you have said that you did not ask Zagreb for permission to go as a volunteer to the HVO. Did you ask anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzanko, who asked me to go there at the time, was a deputy commander of the Army District of Split. I considered it unnecessary to ask anybody else, because he had asked me to go. If somebody of a lower rank had asked me, I would have reported to the commander of the Army District.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That appears -- that appears very plausible. You said that Mr. Dzanko asked you to go there. Do you confirm this? No, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a misinterpretation. I can tell you what my colleague Ms. Lustig, who studied in New York, said to me. It was interpreted: "He asked me to go" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic, this seems to me rather abusive. I asked a question, I got an answer, and now you want to tell me what someone from New York told you?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I just want to say that a correct interpretation would be "who asked me if I wanted to go" rather than "who asked me to go." This is a nuance in the English language. I don't pretend that I have such a master of English. That's why I mentioned my co-worker who is a near-native speaker of English. So I would ask the interpretation to be adjusted accordingly because it correctly reflects what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Anyway, Mr. Beneta, it was not your own initiative, it was not initially your idea to go to the HVO, but it was suggested to you. You were asked whether you would be prepared to go, whether you would -- yes, whether you would be prepared to go; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Dzanko asked me whether I wanted to go with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, if you had said, No, to him, I'm not interested, I don't wish to go, what would have happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing would have happened. I would have continued doing the work I had done until that time, and he would have looked for somebody else. I apologise, but I don't have the English transcript on my left screen, so I cannot see whether the transcript is up to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The usher will check this out. The usher --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] -- many things. I'm putting this question to you for the following reason. A few months ago, we saw a document which stated that soldiers from the Croatian Army had to go to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they didn't want to go. Then these men were prosecuted. How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is news to me. My experience tells otherwise. If you wish, I can give you concrete examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, if I understand correctly, when one is a volunteer, one can decide where one is to be assigned; but if one is a conscript, then one doesn't have a choice. Is that how the Croatian Army functioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to going to Bosnia-Herzegovina and participating in operations there, the Croatian Army participated in an organised fashion in a part of territory along the border, which made sense in the context of defending Croatian territory against the aggression. I spoke about that in detail yesterday, when I spoke about my unit. About all other instances of going there, as far as I know, persons who wanted to went there. And I will be frank and say also that it suited the Croatian authorities to strengthen the defence across the border, where the Croatian authorities had no direct influence. That is why, when I was asked whether I wanted to assist in organising the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I accepted. Likewise, groups of people were sometimes allowed to go there, and they went there in groups. There were situations in which I had to prevent people, Croats born in Croatia, from accompanying their fellow soldiers born in Bosnia-Herzegovina who went there to protect their homes and parents, because out of a feeling of solidarity with them, they wanted to go there, too, and help them, but I, as a commander, had my duties connected with the defence of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Beneta, there's something I don't understand, and I'm sure you will shed some light on this. When you were answering to the question from Judge Trechsel, you said that General Dzanko had asked you whether you were willing to go to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you answered, Yes. We spent the entire morning trying to understand - at least that's what I think was being elicited - that there was a single theatre of war, because you had one enemy, one single enemy, the Serbian forces. I understood that the Republic of Croatia was in jeopardy. In such a case, why did he ask you whether you were willing to go or not? All he had to do was tell you, Mr. Beneta, as of Monday you'll be in Split, and then you will head for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is an order. Please execute the order. Why are you asked whether you were willing to go? I really don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two crucial moments which I, at this moment, consider important, one being that Croatia had entered a clause in its constitution that it would engage in armed combat to defend its territory, Croatia as a successive state of the former Yugoslavia. Only now that we are NATO members will it be allowed to engage in armed combat outside the territory of Croatia. Another reason is that the international community, and I still think that it didn't understand the situation completely, prevented Croatia from doing what you, too, Your Honours, considered logical; namely, to defeat the enemy with allies as soon as possible and thus eliminate the dangers or the threats to a normal development. The policy of the state was such that it didn't allow commanders to take their units to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although there was such demands. I must admit if I had been in a position to decide freely while I was brigade commander, I would have been glad to go to an area in jeopardy, and that would have been welcomed by my fighters, because the Serbian forces had occupied over 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we couldn't do so. That is why there was a political understanding for volunteers to go there, but units were not allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I understood. You're telling us that for political reasons, the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman actually, did not want the Croatian Army to officially be in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so the solution found was to ask soldiers of the HV to volunteer to go to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I cannot say that the Croatian authorities demanded that soldiers go to Bosnia-Herzegovina, but if there should be such demands, it was possible. I said that we were even caught by surprise that 30 to 40 per cent of my fighters all of a sudden wanted to leave my units and go to their homes, where their parents were, and under the pressure of such a situation, we reported up the hierarchy because otherwise there was the threat of them leaving on their own. The situation remained unchanged throughout the war, until the signing of the agreement and the operations we conducted together with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can now suppose that the war would have been much shorter if the agreement had been signed earlier, because it would have provided a political framework in which we would have pushed back the enemy together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me ask the Coric Defence whether it has any questions. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. We have no questions, but we wish to thank the witness for his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, finally, the Pusic Defence. Mr. Ibrisimovic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. I'll now give the floor to Mr. Laws, and I thank him for the binder. This was extremely well organised, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, to each of Your Honours, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
